text: During the summers of 2005 and 2006, the archaeologists discovered a Viking Age longhouse at Hrísbrú, just 10 m northeast of the previously excavated church. The longhouse is more than 27 meters long and 10 meters wide, and appears to be part of the initial habitation of the Hrísbrú farm. In the middle of the longhouse a excavators found a longfire containing ash, charcoal and burnt bone. Post holes with stone linings and void spaces where the posts that held up the roof used to stand were discovered along the inside of the benches. The original posts had been removed after the abandonment of the building, probably for reuse in other structures. The excavated walls of the longhouse are approximately 2 meters thick and consist of turf and stone. One-meter wide benches, where the inhabitants would have worked and slept, span the distance from the walls to the floor. On the earthen floor and benches of the longhouse, the archaeologists found artifacts such as spindle whorls, iron nails and fittings, and several glass and stone beads. These artifacts, some of which can typologically be dated to the Viking Age, reveal the living conditions of the inhabitants and are witnesses from a long-vanished past. Archaeological excavation of the longhouse will continue in the years to come.
